items.prompt: What makes a requirement "falsifiable" in the sense this unit uses the term?
choices: It must be written in formal legal language

There's a concrete, checkable way to determine whether it's been met — someone who wasn't in the original conversation can look at the built thing and the requirement and independently reach the same yes/no answer
It must be approved by a manager before implementation starts
It must be impossible to disagree with
items.explanation: "Improve the dashboard" can't be checked by anyone independently; "initial load under 2 seconds for the 95th percentile" can be — that independent checkability is the specific property falsifiability refers to here.
items.reference:
Vague ask

"Improve the dashboard" — no one can check this independently

Falsifiable requirement

"Load under 2s for the 95th percentile" — anyone can check it

Why: falsifiability means an independent, checkable yes/no answer — not approval, not agreement, not certainty.
items.learnMore:
What "falsifiable" actually means here

A falsifiable requirement is one where a person who wasn't in the original conversation — a new engineer, QA, or the requester six months later — can look at the built thing and the requirement side by side and independently reach the same yes/no answer.

This is different from "specific-sounding." "Make it professional-looking" sounds more specific than "improve it," but it's still not falsifiable — there's no independent check for "professional-looking." A requirement needs an observable, measurable, or enumerable condition, not just more words.

Common mistake

Assuming a requirement is falsifiable because it's detailed or long. Length isn't the test — independent checkability is.

items.prompt: A requirement reads: "the checkout flow should feel modern and professional." Why does this fail the falsifiability test, even though it sounds fairly specific?
choices: It's too short to be a real requirement
It doesn't specify a technology stack
There's no independent, checkable condition — two different reviewers could reasonably disagree about whether it's met, with no way to settle it by looking at the built thing alone
It mentions a subjective feeling, and subjective feelings are always irrelevant to requirements
items.explanation: Falsifiability isn't about sounding specific — it's about whether an independent check is possible. "Modern and professional" invites reasonable disagreement with no way to resolve it by inspection, unlike a load-time threshold or an enumerated field list.
items.reference:
Vague ask

"Improve the dashboard" — no one can check this independently

Falsifiable requirement

"Load under 2s for the 95th percentile" — anyone can check it

Why: falsifiability means an independent, checkable yes/no answer — not approval, not agreement, not certainty.

items.prompt: Six months after a feature ships, the original requester and a new engineer who never saw the original conversation both need to check whether a requirement was actually met. What property of the requirement makes this possible?
choices: The requirement was written by someone senior
The requirement is falsifiable — it states a checkable condition that doesn't depend on remembering or reconstructing the original conversation's context
The requirement is written in the shortest possible sentence
The requirement was verbally agreed upon, which is always sufficient
items.explanation: This is exactly the scenario falsifiability is built for: a requirement that only makes sense to people who were in the room fails the moment those people are no longer available — a falsifiable one still works.

items.prompt: In a user story ("As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]"), why is the "so that" clause described as often the most valuable part?
choices: It's mostly decorative and rarely affects implementation decisions
It lets an engineer make a reasonable judgment call on details the story didn't explicitly specify, by reasoning about what would actually serve the stated reason
It's required by most project management software and has no other purpose
It's only useful for tracking who requested the feature
items.explanation: A filter example shows this directly: whether a filter should reset or stay sticky isn't answerable from the capability alone, but is inferable from the stated reason — the benefit clause fills gaps the explicit spec doesn't cover.
items.reference:
Story pieceWhat it does
"I want [capability]"States the explicit ask
"so that [benefit]"Lets an engineer infer unstated details from the reason

Why: the stated reason is what makes a judgment call on an unlisted detail defensible instead of a guess.
items.learnMore:
Why the reason clause carries more weight than the ask

"As an account reviewer, I want to select multiple accounts and change their status, so that I can process a weekly batch without updating each one individually" — the capability alone doesn't say whether the bulk change needs to log an audit entry. The reason (processing an existing, already-logged workflow faster) does: dropping the log would undermine the very thing the story exists to support.

This is why user stories aren't just a formatting convention. A story with no "so that" clause leaves every unlisted detail as a pure guess; a story with one gives the engineer something to reason from when a detail comes up that the story didn't explicitly cover.

Common mistake

Writing the "so that" clause as an afterthought ("so that it's better") instead of the actual underlying reason — a vague reason clause can't resolve any real ambiguity.

items.prompt: A story says: "As an account reviewer, I want to bulk-change account status, so that I can process a weekly verification batch without updating accounts one at a time." Mid-implementation, the engineer wonders whether the bulk change should create an audit log entry, which the story never mentions. What should the engineer do?
choices: Skip the audit log, since it wasn't explicitly listed

Reason from the "so that" clause: since this replaces an existing workflow that already logs each change, dropping the log would undermine the story's own stated purpose, so it should probably be included — and confirm with the stakeholder if there's any doubt
Add every possible feature that might be useful, regardless of the story
Refuse to build anything until every conceivable detail is listed explicitly
items.explanation: This is the practical value of the "so that" clause: it gives the engineer a principled way to reason about unlisted details, grounded in the stated purpose, rather than guessing blindly or stalling entirely.

items.prompt: Why do acceptance criteria matter, according to this unit's framing of "done"?
choices: They make requirements documents longer, which looks more thorough
Without them, "done" is a private judgment call made separately by the builder and the requester, which is where scope disagreements after the fact come from
They're only useful for legal compliance, not for engineering decisions
They replace the need for a user story entirely
items.explanation: The core argument is about turning two potentially-different private judgment calls into one shared, checkable fact — that's what prevents "I thought this was done" disagreements from surfacing only after delivery.
items.reference:
No acceptance criteria

"Done" is a private judgment call, made twice

With acceptance criteria

"Done" is a shared checklist anyone can verify

Why: two independent judgment calls agreeing is luck, not design — a checklist removes the luck.
items.learnMore:
Why acceptance criteria exist at all

Without a checklist, "done" is decided twice: once by whoever built the feature, and once by whoever asked for it. If those two people's mental picture of "done" doesn't match — which is common, since neither wrote theirs down — the mismatch only surfaces after the work is finished, when it's expensive to fix.

Acceptance criteria convert that private judgment into a shared, explicit, checkable list, agreed on before implementation starts. Scope disagreements that would otherwise surface at delivery time surface instead while the checklist is being written — cheap, not expensive.

Common mistake

Treating acceptance criteria as a nice-to-have for "important" features only. The size of a request has no bearing on how much implicit disagreement about "done" it can hide.

items.prompt: A story ships with no written acceptance criteria. The requester says it's not done; the engineer says it is. What does this unit say actually went wrong?
choices: The engineer clearly made a mistake somewhere in the implementation
Two separate, unwritten judgment calls about what "done" means were never reconciled before the work started, so the disagreement only surfaced at the end instead of being resolved cheaply up front
The requester is being unreasonable and should accept the engineer's judgment
This kind of disagreement is unavoidable no matter what process is used
items.explanation: This is exactly the failure mode acceptance criteria exist to prevent — not by making anyone more careful, but by making "done" an explicit, shared artifact agreed on before implementation instead of two separate private opinions.

items.prompt: A stakeholder says: "We need bulk actions on the admin panel." Why is this framed as a risky requirement to build from directly?
choices: Because stakeholders are usually wrong about what they want

Because it already smuggles in an assumed solution shape (bulk-delete-style actions), and building directly from it skips confirming whether that's actually the right operation for the underlying need
Because "bulk actions" is grammatically ambiguous
Because admin panels should never have bulk actions
items.explanation: The risk isn't that the stakeholder is wrong to want something — it's that the ask already names a specific mechanism (bulk actions, which reads as delete-style to most engineers) before the actual underlying need (bulk status changes) has been confirmed.
items.reference:
First-offered solution

"We need bulk actions" (implies: like the delete pattern seen elsewhere)

Underlying need

"We need to verify 30-50 accounts/week without one-by-one clicking"

Why: the first-offered solution is one guess at meeting the need — probing finds the need itself, which may point to a different solution.
items.learnMore:
Why stakeholders describe solutions, not needs

Stakeholders naturally describe what they imagine the fix looks like, not the underlying constraint that fix is meant to solve — this isn't a flaw in how they communicate, it's just how most people think about problems: in terms of a plausible fix, not an abstracted need.

"We need bulk actions" already smuggled in an assumption (that deletion-style bulk actions were the right shape). Requirements gathering has to actively probe past that first offer — asking what workflow it replaces, not just accepting the proposed mechanism — or the resulting spec just encodes someone's first guess as if it were a requirement.

Common mistake

Treating the stakeholder's literal proposed solution as the requirement, instead of treating it as one data point about the underlying need that still needs to be confirmed.

items.prompt: What is the practical difference between "probing for the underlying need" and "just building what was asked for"?
choices: There is no real difference — both produce the same result

Probing asks what workflow or constraint the proposed solution is meant to serve, which can reveal that a different operation (bulk status change, not bulk delete) actually serves that need better than the literally-requested one
Probing means refusing to build anything until the stakeholder writes their own detailed spec
Building what was asked for is always faster and therefore always the right call
items.explanation: Probing isn't about second-guessing the stakeholder for its own sake — it's about confirming the proposed mechanism actually matches the real underlying need before committing implementation time to it.

items.prompt: Why does resolving ambiguity during requirements gathering cost so much less than resolving it after implementation?
choices: It doesn't actually cost less; the total cost is the same either way

Ambiguity that isn't resolved up front doesn't disappear — it moves downstream to wherever someone first has to make a concrete decision, and by then the cost includes whatever implementation work has to be redone, not just the cost of the original clarifying conversation
Because clarifying conversations always take longer than implementation work
Requirements gathering has no effect on eventual implementation cost
items.explanation: The ambiguity itself is the same either way — what changes is when and how expensively it gets resolved. A clarifying question costs minutes; discovering the same ambiguity in QA or after shipping costs the implementation cycle built on the wrong assumption.
items.reference:
When resolvedRelative cost
Same conversation~1x (the conversation itself)
Code reviewA few times the conversation
QA / after shipTens of times the conversation

Why: the ambiguity doesn't vanish if unresolved — it moves downstream and accumulates whatever was built on top of it.
items.learnMore:
Why ambiguity compounds instead of staying flat

An unresolved ambiguity doesn't disappear when a team skips straight to building an assumed interpretation — it just waits for whoever first has to make a concrete decision. If that's the implementing engineer, the cost is small: a guess. If it's QA, the cost includes whatever was built on the wrong guess. If it's the stakeholder after ship, the cost includes everything built on the guess, plus however long the tool didn't help them.

This is the entire practical argument for spending real time on requirements gathering: it's not that ambiguity is always cheap to resolve — it's that its cost is not fixed, and gets strictly worse (often non-linearly) the later it's caught.

Common mistake

Treating requirements gathering as overhead to minimize, on the theory that any time not spent building is wasted. The time isn't wasted — it's the cheapest point at which the ambiguity can ever be resolved.

items.prompt: An engineer argues that skipping requirements clarification saves time because "we can always fix it later if it's wrong." What's the flaw in this reasoning, per this unit?
choices: There's no flaw — this is generally good advice

"Fixing it later" isn't the same cost as getting it right up front — the fix has to also undo or rework whatever was built on the wrong assumption, and that cost grows the longer the wrong assumption stood
Fixing things later is always impossible, so this approach never works
This is only a problem for very large features, not small ones
items.explanation: The flaw isn't that fixing later is impossible — it's that it's never the same price as getting it right the first time, because by "later" there's usually real work sitting on top of the wrong assumption that also has to be undone.

items.prompt: In the cost-of-delayed-discovery chart, why does the same underlying gap in knowledge cost roughly 40x more when caught after ship than when caught in the original conversation?
choices: Because post-ship bugs are inherently more complex to understand
Because the cost isn't just the original gap — it includes whatever implementation, testing, and real-world impact accumulated on top of the wrong assumption before it was caught
Because customers charge penalty fees for late fixes
The 40x figure is arbitrary and doesn't reflect anything real
items.explanation: The gap itself (e.g. "bulk delete vs. bulk status change") is identical at every point on the curve — what changes is how much has been built on the wrong assumption by the time it's caught, and that accumulated work is what the multiplier reflects.
items.reference:
Discovery pointRelative cost (x conversation)
Same conversation1x
Code review3x
QA12x
2 weeks post-ship40x

Why: the same gap in knowledge costs a different amount purely based on how much was built on top of it before it was caught.
items.learnMore:
Reading the cost curve

The chart isn't saying ambiguity is bad — it's saying timing is what determines cost. The underlying gap (e.g. "is this bulk delete or bulk status change?") is identical in every column; only when it's caught changes, and that alone accounts for a 40x spread.

This is why requirements gathering isn't framed as a nice-to-have process step — it's framed as the cheapest point in the entire lifecycle at which this specific cost will ever be paid.

Common mistake

Assuming the curve implies ambiguity should always be eliminated to zero before starting. The claim is narrower: resolve it as early as practical, not that every last unknown must be nailed down first.

items.prompt: What is the main practical implication of the cost-of-delayed-discovery relationship, for how a team should treat requirements gathering?

The relationship implies QA should be removed since it catches problems too late anyway
The relationship only applies to large, complex features

items.prompt: What turns "make the dashboard faster" into "initial load completes in under 2 seconds on a typical connection, for the 95th percentile of users"?
choices: Making the sentence longer
Answering what's being measured, how much is enough, and for which population — the three things a vague ask usually leaves unspecified
Getting sign-off from a manager
Replacing the word "faster" with a synonym
items.explanation: The transformation isn't about length or wording — it's about closing the three specific gaps a vague ask like "faster" leaves open: what metric, what threshold, and for whom.
items.reference:
Vague ask

"Make the dashboard faster"

Falsifiable requirement

"Initial load under 2s for the 95th percentile of users on a typical connection"

Why: the right column names a specific measurement, population, and threshold — the left column names none of the three.
items.learnMore:
The three things a falsifiable requirement usually pins down

Turning a vague ask into a falsifiable requirement usually means answering three questions: what exactly is being measured (load time, not "speed" in general), how much is enough (under 2 seconds, not just "faster"), and for whom (the 95th percentile, not "users" in the abstract, since averages hide bad experiences for a meaningful slice of people).

Skipping any one of the three still leaves room for disagreement later — "under 2 seconds" without a population still leaves open whether that's the average, the typical case, or every single user, and those are very different engineering targets.

Common mistake

Stopping at just adding a number ("faster, under 2 seconds") without also pinning down what's measured and for whom — a number alone isn't automatically falsifiable if its scope is still ambiguous.

items.prompt: A requirement says "the page should load in under 2 seconds," with no mention of which users or what network conditions. Why might this still not be fully falsifiable?
choices: It is already fully falsifiable as written

Because "for which users, under what conditions" is still unanswered — under 2 seconds for the average user on fiber is a very different engineering target than for the 95th percentile on a typical connection
Because 2 seconds is always too slow for a modern site
Because load time can never really be measured precisely
items.explanation: A number alone doesn't guarantee falsifiability if its scope (which users, what conditions) is still open — two engineers could hit "under 2 seconds" in very different, non-equivalent ways without a stated population.

items.prompt: Why does the full "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]" format carry more information than just stating the capability?
choices: It doesn't — the role and reason are just formatting conventions with no functional purpose
The role signals whose existing workflow and expectations are relevant, and the reason signals what the feature needs to preserve from what it's replacing — both are needed to infer unstated details
It's required purely for tracking purposes in project management tools
Longer stories are always better regardless of content
items.explanation: Both the role and the reason do real inferential work: the role anchors whose existing context matters, and the reason anchors what unstated behaviors (like audit logging) should probably carry over from what's being replaced.
items.reference:
Capability only

"Bulk-change account status" — no context for edge cases

Role + capability + reason

"As a reviewer, I want to bulk-change status, so I can process a weekly batch" — edge cases inferable

Why: the role grounds who's affected, the reason grounds what unstated details should probably hold true.
items.learnMore:
Why all three parts of the format matter, not just the capability

The full format — role, capability, reason — is doing more than the capability alone would. The role ("account reviewer") signals whose workflow this affects and what their existing habits and expectations probably are. The reason ("process a weekly batch without one-by-one updates") signals what the feature needs to preserve from the existing process it's replacing.

A story that only states the capability ("select multiple accounts, change status") loses both of these — an engineer reading just that has no way to infer whether existing behaviors like audit logging should carry over, because there's no stated reason to reason from.

Common mistake

Treating the role and reason clauses as boilerplate to fill in mechanically, rather than actual information the rest of the story depends on for resolving ambiguity.

items.prompt: A story is written as just "Bulk-change account status" with no role or reason attached. What's the risk in building directly from this?
choices: There's no risk — a capability alone is always sufficient
The engineer has no stated context to infer unlisted-but-implied details from, such as whether the existing single-item audit logging behavior should carry over to the bulk version
The risk is purely stylistic, not functional
The story would be rejected automatically by any tracking tool
items.explanation: Without the role and reason, there's nothing to reason from when an unlisted detail comes up mid-implementation — the engineer is left guessing instead of inferring from a stated context and purpose.

items.prompt: Why does the bulk-status-change story's acceptance criteria explicitly include "Bulk delete is explicitly OUT of scope for this story," rather than just omitting any mention of delete?
choices: It's unnecessary — omitting delete already makes it clear it's not included
Stating the exclusion explicitly removes any ambiguity that omission alone could leave, especially since the original vague ask ("bulk actions") plausibly implied deletion in the first place
It's a legal requirement for all acceptance criteria
It makes the checklist look more thorough without adding real value
items.explanation: Omission and explicit exclusion aren't equivalent — different readers can fill a silent gap differently. Given that "bulk actions" already suggested deletion to the engineer in Path A, stating the exclusion explicitly closes exactly that risk.
items.reference:
No checklist

Scope (e.g. "is delete included?") stays implicit, assumed differently by different people

Explicit checklist

Scope is explicit, including what's deliberately excluded ("bulk delete is OUT of scope")

Why: writing down what's explicitly excluded prevents it from being silently assumed included by either side.
items.learnMore:
Why acceptance criteria should state exclusions, not just inclusions

A checklist that only lists what should be true ("multi-select checkboxes exist," "status updates apply to all selected") still leaves room for disagreement about anything it doesn't mention. Explicitly stating "bulk delete is OUT of scope for this story" closes that gap directly, rather than leaving it to be assumed.

This matters most exactly where the original vague ask was most likely to be misread — "bulk actions" plausibly implied deletion to begin with, so the acceptance criteria that resolve that specific ambiguity are worth stating explicitly, not just implying by omission.

Common mistake

Writing acceptance criteria only as a list of what to build, and assuming anything unmentioned is obviously excluded — omission is not the same as an explicit statement, and readers fill silence differently.

items.prompt: A checklist for a new feature lists five things that should be true when it's done, but says nothing about what's excluded. What risk does this leave open?
choices: No risk — a list of inclusions is always sufficient
Anything not mentioned can still be silently assumed included by one side and excluded by the other, since silence doesn't resolve ambiguity the way an explicit statement does
The checklist is now too long to be useful
This only matters for features with security implications
items.explanation: A list of inclusions alone doesn't address scope boundaries — anything left unmentioned is still open to being interpreted differently by different readers, which is exactly what explicit exclusions are meant to prevent.

items.prompt: What's a practical test for whether a written requirement is actually falsifiable?
choices: Whether everyone currently on the team agrees with it right now
Whether someone who wasn't in the original conversation could look at the built feature and the requirement and independently reach the same yes/no answer, without needing extra unwritten context
Whether it was approved in a formal document
Whether it uses precise, technical-sounding vocabulary
items.explanation: Current team agreement isn't the test — memory fades and people change teams. The real test is whether the requirement stands on its own for someone with no access to the original conversation.
items.reference:
Depends on context

"Looks fine" — only makes sense to people who were in the original conversation

Independently checkable

"Multi-select, status change, audit log per change" — checkable by anyone reading the built feature

Why: the test for a good requirement is whether someone outside the original conversation reaches the same yes/no answer.
items.learnMore:
The independent-checker test

A useful way to test whether a requirement is actually falsifiable: imagine someone who wasn't in the original conversation — a new engineer, QA, or the original requester six months later — looking at the built feature and the requirement side by side. Can they reach a yes/no answer without needing to ask anyone what was originally meant?

If the answer depends on remembering unwritten context from the original conversation, the requirement isn't actually falsifiable yet, no matter how confident everyone in that original conversation feels about what was meant.

Common mistake

Assuming a requirement is fine because everyone currently on the team agrees on what it means. Team membership and memory both change — a requirement should stand on its own.

items.prompt: A requirement is considered "done" by everyone who was in the original planning conversation. Six months later, a new QA engineer, with no access to that conversation, can't tell from the written requirement whether a specific edge case was in or out of scope. What does this indicate?
choices: Nothing is wrong — the requirement was fine for the people who wrote it
The requirement wasn't actually falsifiable in the first place — it relied on shared unwritten context that doesn't survive when the people or their memory of the conversation are no longer available
The new QA engineer should just ask around until they find someone who remembers
This is an inevitable and acceptable cost of software development
items.explanation: This is the exact failure the independent-checker test is designed to catch — a requirement that only works for people who were in the room isn't actually falsifiable, it just hasn't been tested against someone outside that room yet.

items.prompt: In Request 1, why did Sam build a fully working feature that still wasn't what Elena needed?
choices: Because Sam was careless or didn't test the feature properly

Because "bulk actions" was never specified beyond two words in a ticket, and Sam filled the gap with the most common pattern he'd seen elsewhere (bulk delete) rather than Elena's actual workflow (bulk status changes)
Because Elena changed her mind after the feature shipped
Because Sam intentionally built the wrong thing to save time
items.explanation: Sam's implementation was genuinely correct for the requirement he assumed — the failure was in the unspecified requirement itself, not the code. Filling an ambiguous ask with a plausible-but-unverified assumption is exactly the trap requirements gathering exists to prevent.
items.reference:
Request 1 builtWhat Elena needed
Multi-select + delete buttonMulti-select + status change
Confirmation dialog for deletionNo deletion at all — not her workflow
0 clarifying questions askedWould've taken ~10 minutes to ask

Why: Sam's implementation was genuinely correct — correct for a guessed requirement that was never confirmed against Elena's real workflow.
items.learnMore:
The gap was upstream of the code, not in it

Sam's bulk-delete feature worked exactly as built: multi-select, confirmation, deletion. Every line of it did what it was supposed to do. The problem was never in the implementation — it was that "bulk actions" was never actually specified beyond two words in a ticket, and Sam filled that gap with the most common pattern he'd seen elsewhere, rather than Elena's actual, un-asked-about workflow.

This is the core lesson Request 1 illustrates: a wrong requirement produces a correctly-built wrong feature, and no amount of careful coding, testing, or code review catches that — those all check whether the built thing matches the spec, not whether the spec matches the real need.

Common mistake

Treating Request 1's outcome as evidence Sam should have been more careful. The fix isn't more careful coding — it's confirming the requirement before any coding starts.

items.prompt: Could code review or QA testing have caught Request 1's mismatch before it reached Elena?
choices: Yes, thorough code review always catches wrong requirements
Not reliably — code review and QA typically check whether the built thing matches the assumed spec, not whether the spec itself matches the real, unconfirmed need; the gap was upstream of both
No, this kind of mismatch is theoretically impossible to catch at any stage
Only automated tests could have caught this, not human review
items.explanation: Code review and QA are effective at catching implementation bugs — deviations from the spec — but neither is designed to catch a spec that itself doesn't match reality, since neither activity typically re-verifies the original requirement against the stakeholder's actual need.

items.prompt: Request 2 asked one clarifying question and got a real, useful answer. Why did the resulting feature still ship with a compliance gap?
choices: Because Elena lied about her workflow

Because Sam's single question resolved which operation was needed (status change, not delete) but didn't probe for other implicit requirements, like the existing audit-logging norm Elena didn't think to restate unprompted
Because audit logging is impossible to implement for bulk operations
Because Sam implemented the status change incorrectly
items.explanation: One good question narrows ambiguity — it doesn't guarantee it's fully resolved. Elena's answer about the workflow was accurate and complete for what was asked; the audit-log requirement simply wasn't covered by that specific question.
items.reference:
Request 2 learnedRequest 2 missed
The operation: status change, not deleteWhether "suspended" also needed to be supported
The batch size: 30-50/weekThe scale limit and audit-log requirement
Real progress over Request 1Still stopped one round too early

Why: one good question is real progress, but stopping after the first answer still leaves ambiguity uncaught.
items.learnMore:
Why one clarifying question wasn't enough

Request 2's single question ("what workflow does this replace?") genuinely fixed the biggest problem from Request 1 — Sam now builds the right operation. But Sam stopped there, and Elena's first answer didn't happen to mention the audit-log requirement, because to her it's just how status changes already work — not something she'd think to restate unless asked directly.

This illustrates that a good first question narrows the gap without necessarily closing it. The remaining gap (audit logging, plus which statuses) only surfaces with a second, more targeted round of questions — which is what Request 3 adds.

Common mistake

Treating "I asked a clarifying question" as equivalent to "I've resolved the ambiguity." One question can resolve one specific ambiguity while leaving others, especially implicit ones, completely untouched.

items.prompt: What's the practical lesson from comparing Request 2 to Request 3?
choices: Asking any clarifying question at all is pointless if it doesn't catch everything

A good question is genuine progress, but requirements gathering usually needs more than one round — the first answer often resolves one ambiguity while leaving others, especially unstated norms, still open
Request 2's stakeholder was less cooperative than Request 3's
The number of questions asked doesn't matter, only their phrasing
items.explanation: Request 2 wasn't a failure — it was real progress over Request 1. The lesson is that requirements gathering often needs a second round, because a stakeholder's first answer addresses the question asked, not necessarily every relevant unstated norm.

items.prompt: Why did Request 3's conversation surface the audit-log requirement, when Elena's original ticket never mentioned it?
choices: Sam guessed it was needed based on general best practices, unrelated to the conversation

A targeted question about what needs to happen after the update surfaced an existing norm (audit logs for single-item status changes) that Elena assumed would silently carry over to the bulk version, and wouldn't have thought to restate unprompted
Audit logging is always a mandatory requirement for every feature, regardless of context
Elena explicitly listed it in the very first ticket
items.explanation: This illustrates a specific value of targeted questions: implicit, existing norms (like requiring an audit log, already true for single-item changes) are exactly the kind of requirement a stakeholder won't think to restate because it feels obvious to them — but it isn't obvious to someone building a new bulk pathway from scratch.
items.reference:
Not asked

Elena never restates the audit-log norm unprompted — it's just how things already work

Asked

Sam asks: "anything that needs to happen after the update — a log entry — for compliance?"

Why: existing norms are exactly what stakeholders won't think to restate — because to them it's already obvious, not because they're hiding it.
items.learnMore:
Why targeted questions surface norms a stakeholder wouldn't think to mention

The audit-log requirement wasn't a secret Elena was withholding — it simply wasn't relevant to the questions Sam had asked so far. From Elena's point of view, of course a status change gets logged; that's already true for every single-item change today, so it doesn't occur to her as something that needs restating for the bulk version.

This is a specific, recurring value of targeted follow-up questions: they surface implicit, already-existing norms that a stakeholder assumes will silently carry over, but that an engineer building a new pathway from scratch has no way to know about unless it's explicitly asked.

Common mistake

Assuming a stakeholder would have mentioned an important constraint if it were really important. Obviousness to the stakeholder is exactly why it goes unmentioned, not evidence it doesn't matter.

items.prompt: What kind of requirement is an "implicit norm," in the sense the audit-log example illustrates?
choices: A requirement that's written down somewhere but easy to miss
An existing behavior or rule the stakeholder considers so obvious and already-true that they don't think to state it explicitly for a new feature that logically extends the same workflow
A requirement that only applies to compliance-heavy industries
A requirement invented by the engineer, not the stakeholder
items.explanation: An implicit norm is exactly this: true and assumed by the stakeholder, but never stated, because from their perspective it's already an established fact about how things work, not a new decision to communicate.

items.prompt: What's wrong with an acceptance criterion like "use a Set to track selected IDs"?
choices: Nothing — implementation details make acceptance criteria more precise

It describes HOW the feature is built rather than an observable, checkable BEHAVIOR — a good acceptance criterion should be verifiable by someone who never looks at the code, the same falsifiability test from L2
Sets are an inefficient data structure and shouldn't be used regardless
Acceptance criteria should never mention any technical concepts at all
items.explanation: This is a flagged failure mode: the point of acceptance criteria is independently checkable observable behavior, and "use a Set" describes an internal implementation choice that a non-code-reading reviewer couldn't verify against the running feature.
items.reference:
Implementation-described

"Use a Set to track selected IDs"

Behavior-described

"Selecting an account and deselecting it removes it from the batch"

Why: a criterion should be checkable by someone who never looks at the code — the falsifiability test from L2, applied to acceptance criteria specifically.
items.learnMore:
Why acceptance criteria should describe behavior, not implementation

"Use a Set to track selected IDs" tells you something about how the code might be organized internally, but nothing about what the feature actually does from a user's point of view — and it can't be checked by anyone who isn't reading the code.

A criterion phrased as observable behavior ("selecting and then deselecting an account removes it from the batch") can be verified by clicking through the running feature, by QA, by the original stakeholder, or by a future engineer — none of whom need to see a single line of code. That's the same falsifiability test from L2, applied specifically to how acceptance criteria should be worded.

Common mistake

Writing criteria that describe a specific internal data structure or algorithm as if that were the requirement — it constrains implementation choices without adding any actual checkability.

items.prompt: Which of these two acceptance criteria correctly describes observable behavior rather than implementation?
choices: "Store selected account IDs in a Set for O(1) lookup"
"Deselecting a previously-selected account removes it from the batch that will be updated"
"Use a hash map keyed by account ID"
"Implement the selection state using React's useState hook"
items.explanation: The second option describes what a user or tester can observe by using the feature — no code-reading required. The other three all describe internal data structures or specific technical choices, none of which are independently checkable by someone outside the implementation.

items.prompt: "Bulk actions on the admin panel" is two words. Why did it still need three separate rounds of questions to resolve?
choices: Because Elena was being deliberately vague
Because the length of a request has no relationship to how much ambiguity it contains — a short ask can hide just as many unresolved unknowns (operation, scale, side effects) as a much longer one
Because Sam is an inexperienced engineer who needed extra help
Because admin panel features are always unusually complex
items.explanation: The size of the request text has no bearing on the amount of ambiguity it hides — "bulk actions" was short precisely because the words that would have disambiguated it (which operation, what scale) were exactly what was missing.
items.reference:
Short request

"We need bulk actions on the admin panel" — two words describing the feature

Actual ambiguity

Operation? Scale? Audit log? Deletion in scope? — 4+ real unknowns

Why: the size of the request text has no relationship to how much ambiguity it hides.
items.learnMore:
Why a two-word ask can hide as much ambiguity as a two-paragraph one

"Bulk actions" is short specifically because it's vague — the words that would disambiguate it (which operation, what scale, what side effects) are exactly the words that are missing. A longer, more detailed-sounding request isn't automatically less ambiguous, and a short one isn't automatically simple.

The right way to size a requirements-gathering conversation is by the actual number of unresolved unknowns the request contains, discovered by asking, not by how many words the original ask used. A two-word ticket that hides four real unknowns needs the same conversation a longer one with four real unknowns would.

Common mistake

Skipping clarification for small-sounding requests on the assumption that "it's simple, I'll just build it." Simplicity of phrasing and simplicity of scope are two different things.

items.learnMore:
Why requirements aren't frozen once gathered

The three-request conversation resolves the ambiguity that was knowable at the time it happened. But implementation itself can surface genuinely new information — for instance, discovering the account list has 10,000+ rows, which makes an unpaginated multi-select impractical in a way nobody anticipated during the original conversation.

The right move when this happens is the same move that worked the first time: go back to the stakeholder with the new, concrete information, rather than silently picking an interpretation and hoping it's close enough. Treating the original requirements conversation as a one-time, now-frozen event repeats exactly the mistake Request 1 made, just later in the process.

Common mistake

Assuming that because requirements were gathered once, any new complication discovered mid-build should just be handled by engineering judgment alone, without looping the stakeholder back in.
